mainTopic: רב ספרא's rule on which interest our courts return, and three explanations of the משנה about wheat owed as wine
overview: The גמרא finishes defending רב ספרא's rule that our courts return interest exactly where non-Jewish courts would collect it. רב אשי explains that non-Jewish courts treat a lender's field as a sale, not a loan. The גמרא then explains the rule's two halves. רבית קצוצה is collected by their courts and returned by ours, as רבי אלעזר holds. רבית מוקדמת and רבית מאוחרת are collected by neither and not returned. Next the גמרא turns to the משנה about wheat bought at a דינר זהב per כור and later owed as wine, and asks why it matters that the seller has no wine. רבה says it is a case of turning a debt into a purchase, but אביי objects that this would apply even if the seller had wine. אביי instead reads the משנה through רב ספרא's ברייתא about loans disguised as wheat sales. רבא challenges אביי's reading with several wording problems, and the last one, the market-price language, cannot be fixed. רבא then begins his own explanation, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: End of the challenge: our law does not return this interest
steps.stepSummary: The challenge ends by pointing out that in this case our law does not make the lender return anything to the borrower.
steps.simpleTranslation: And yet by our laws, we do not make the lender return it to the borrower.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the last line of a challenge that began before this section. The challenger points out a case where our law does NOT make the lender give the money back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב ספרא's rule ties the two legal systems together. The challenger brought a case, a field held by the lender who eats its produce, where non-Jewish courts would act, yet our courts do not force a return. If that is true, the two systems don't line up, and the rule breaks.

phrases.english: And by our laws we do not return
phrases.notes: This is the end of a question that started earlier. The case is a field the lender holds and eats the produce from.

phrases.english: from the lender to the borrower.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּבְדִינֵינוּ אֵין מַחְזִירִין מִמַּלְוֶה לְלֹוֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes a challenge that began before this section.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ספרא's rule that the two legal systems match
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A case where non-Jewish law acts but our law does not force a return would break the match between the systems.

steps.title: They see it as a sale, not a loan
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that the non-Jewish courts view the field as having been sold to the lender, so for them it is not interest at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: For them, the field came into the lender's hands as a sale.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי defends רב ספרא's rule. He says the non-Jewish courts don't treat this case as a loan with interest at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the non-Jewish system sees the deal as a temporary sale, the lender eats the produce as an owner, not as someone taking interest. So this case is not really a case of 'interest by their laws', and it does not contradict the rule.

keyTerms.meaning: in the form of a sale

phrases.english: He said to him: They,
phrases.notes: The one answering is רב אשי. 'They' means the non-Jewish courts.

phrases.english: it came into their hands in the form of a sale.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִינְהוּ, בְּתוֹרַת זְבִינֵי אֲתָא לִידַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case: it is a sale, not a loan, in their system
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Non-Jewish law treats the field as interest on a loan, so the systems don't match.
steps.terutzMaskana: Non-Jewish law sees it as a sale, so it is not a case of interest at all and the rule stands.

steps.title: Then what does רב ספרא's rule teach?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if each case can be explained away like this, what is the point of רב ספרא's rule?
steps.simpleTranslation: But then, the rule 'any case where by their laws' that רב ספרא says, what is it coming to teach us?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now questions the rule itself. If cases keep turning out to be different from each other, what does the rule actually add?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once we say the non-Jewish system looks at deals in its own way, comparing the two systems seems to tell us nothing. So the גמרא asks what practical lesson the rule gives. This sets up the answer in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: what is he coming to teach us?

phrases.english: But 'any case where by their laws,'
that רב ספרא is saying:
what is he coming to teach us?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא כֹּל שֶׁאִילּוּ בְּדִינֵיהֶן, דְּקָאָמַר רַב סָפְרָא: מַאי אֲתָא לְאַשְׁמוֹעִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After defending the rule, the גמרא asks what the rule is for.
steps.kashyaTarget: The usefulness of רב ספרא's rule
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If each system can see a deal differently, comparing them seems to teach nothing.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What practical lesson רב ספרא's rule teaches, given רב אשי's answer

steps.title: Fixed interest must be given back
steps.stepSummary: The rule's first half is about רבית קצוצה: non-Jewish courts collect it, and our courts force the lender to return it, as רבי אלעזר holds.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what he teaches: any case where their laws take money from the borrower for the lender, our laws take it back from the lender for the borrower. Which case is that? Fixed interest, following רבי אלעזר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the first half of רב ספרא's rule. It refers to interest that was set as part of the loan.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבית קצוצה is interest agreed on from the start. A non-Jewish court would enforce it for the lender. Our court does the opposite and makes the lender return it, which fits רבי אלעזר's view that such interest can be taken back in court.

keyTerms.meaning: they take money out of someone's hands by court order
fixed interest, set as part of the loan deal
the תנא/אמורא who holds fixed interest is taken back by the court

steps.whyThisMatters: It tells us which interest a בית דין actually forces the lender to give back.

phrases.english: This is what he comes to teach us:
any case where by their laws
they take from the borrower for the lender,
by our laws we return from the lender to the borrower,
and what is that? Fixed interest,
and this follows רבי אלעזר.
phrases.notes: רבי אלעזר holds that fixed interest is taken back by the judges.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכִי אֲתָא לְאַשְׁמוֹעִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 3.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What practical lesson רב ספרא's rule gives
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Fixed interest, which non-Jewish courts collect, must be returned by our courts, as רבי אלעזר holds.

steps.title: Interest before or after the loan is not given back
steps.stepSummary: The rule's second half is about רבית מוקדמת and רבית מאוחרת: non-Jewish courts don't collect them, and our courts don't force a return.
steps.simpleTranslation: Any case where by their laws they do not take it from the borrower, by our laws we do not make the lender return it. That is interest paid before the loan and interest paid after it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes explaining רב ספרא's rule with its second half. It names the kinds of interest our court will not take back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבית מוקדמת is a gift given before the loan to get the lender to agree. רבית מאוחרת is a thank-you gift after paying back. Both are forbidden, but since they were not part of the loan deal, no court collects them and our court does not force the lender to return them.

keyTerms.meaning: interest given before the loan, to get the loan
interest given after paying back, as thanks

steps.whatToRemember: רב ספרא's rule: interest that is part of the deal (רבית קצוצה) is collected by their courts and returned by ours. Interest before or after the loan is collected by neither, and not returned by ours.
steps.confusionAlert: Not being returned in court does not mean it is allowed. רבית מוקדמת and מאוחרת are still forbidden; the court just doesn't force a return.

phrases.english: Any case where by their laws they do not take it out,
by our laws we do not return it:
interest paid in advance, interest paid afterward.

steps.triggerLanguage: כֹּל שֶׁאִילּוּ בְּדִינֵיהֶם אֵין מוֹצִיאִין, בְּדִינֵינוּ אֵין מַחְזִירִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the answer started in step 4 with the second half of the rule.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the second half of רב ספרא's rule covers
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Interest paid before the loan or after it, which no court returns.

steps.title: The משנה's case: wheat bought for a gold דינר per כור
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה: someone buys wheat at one gold דינר per כור, which was the market price then.
steps.simpleTranslation: How so? He bought wheat from him at one gold דינר per כור, and that was the market price, and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new part of the משנה and quotes its example. This sets up the question in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The buyer paid ahead for wheat to be given later, at the fair price of that time. The rest of the משנה (marked by 'וכו׳') says the price went up and the seller offered to pay in wine instead, though he has no wine. That is where the question of interest comes in.

keyTerms.meaning: a gold דינר, worth 25 silver דינרים

phrases.english: How so? He bought wheat from him
at a gold דינר per כור,
and such was the market price, etc.
phrases.notes: 'Etc.' points to the rest of the משנה: the price rose, and the seller offered wine he doesn't have.

steps.triggerLanguage: כֵּיצַד: לָקַח הֵימֶנּוּ חִטִּים בְּדִינַר זָהָב הַכּוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new topic: the גמרא returns to the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The משנה's case of wheat bought at the market price to be given later, which then becomes a wine debt.

steps.title: Why does it matter that he has no wine?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the משנה cares whether the seller has wine.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if he has no wine, what of it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks about one detail in the משנה: the seller has no wine. Why should that change anything?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה seems to forbid the deal because the seller lacks wine. The גמרא wants to know why owning wine or not would decide whether this counts as interest. Step 8 sharpens the question, and רבה answers it in step 9.

keyTerms.meaning: what of it? why does it matter?

phrases.aramaic: וְכִי אֵין לוֹ יַיִן, מַאי הָוֵי?
phrases.english: And if he has no wine, what of it?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי אֵין לוֹ יַיִן, מַאי הָוֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about a detail in the משנה quoted in step 6.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the seller's lack of wine matters for the law of interest

steps.title: A ברייתא says having the produce does not matter
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא sharpens its question with a ברייתא: once the market price is publicized, one may set a price even if the seller has none of the produce, since others have it.
steps.simpleTranslation: But a ברייתא teaches: you may not fix a price for produce until the market price is publicized. Once the market price is out, you may fix a price, because even if this seller doesn't have the produce, someone else does!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up its question from step 7 with a ברייתא. That ברייתא suggests the משנה's detail that the seller has no wine should not matter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to the ברייתא, once there is a known market price, the seller can always go buy the produce from someone else. So whether he personally owns any is irrelevant. Why, then, does the משנה make a point of saying the seller has no wine?

keyTerms.meaning: Fixing a price now for produce to be delivered later
The market price has been publicized
This one doesn't have it, but that one does

phrases.english: But isn't it taught in a ברייתא: one may not fix a price for produce
until the market price comes out.
Once the market price has come out, one may fix a price,

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין לָזֶה, יֵשׁ לָזֶה!
phrases.english: for even if this one doesn't have it, that one does!
phrases.notes: "That one" is any other seller in the market, from whom this seller could buy the produce at the known price.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies a source that turns the question of step 7 into a real challenge
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's detail that the seller has no wine
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא permits fixing a price once the market rate is known even when the seller lacks the goods, so lacking wine should not make the deal forbidden.

steps.title: רבה: the משנה is about turning a debt into a purchase
steps.stepSummary: רבה answers that the משנה deals with a case where the seller takes on a debt for the value of the goods.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: In our משנה we are dealing with someone who comes to owe money for their value.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה answers the challenge. He says the משנה is a special kind of case, not an ordinary sale with a fixed price.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, the wheat owed is turned into a money debt, and that debt is then used to "buy" wine for later. If the seller had wine, he could hand it over right away. Since he has none, the deal becomes a debt that grows over time, which looks like רבית.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who answers the question
Comes to become a debtor for their value

phrases.english: רבה said:
In our משנה, we are dealing with one who comes to owe money for their value.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה: מַתְנִיתִין בְּבָא לָחוּב בִּדְמֵיהֶן עָסְקִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 8
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case of the משנה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה is an ordinary sale with a set price, so lacking wine should not matter
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה is about converting an existing debt into a future purchase, which is different from an ordinary sale

steps.title: Support from a ברייתא about a creditor taking future wheat
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא forbids a creditor from taking wheat over twelve months at today's price in place of his money, because no fresh coin was paid.
steps.simpleTranslation: As a ברייתא teaches: Someone was owed a מנה by his friend. He went and stood by the friend's granary and said, "Give me my money, because I want to buy wheat with it." The friend said, "I have wheat that I'll give you. Go figure out how much I owe you at today's price, and I'll deliver it to you over the full twelve months." This is forbidden, because it is not like a case where his coin came into the seller's hand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to support רבה. It shows that using an old debt to pay for future produce is forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, fixing a price at the market rate is allowed because the buyer pays real money now. Here the creditor pays nothing new; he just turns his old loan into future wheat. Since no actual coin changed hands, it is treated as a loan that grows in value, which is רבית.

keyTerms.meaning: A creditor, someone who is owed money
Like a case where his coin has come into his hand, meaning real payment was given

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the key idea for רבה: paying for future goods with an old debt is not a real sale, so it falls under רבית.

phrases.aramaic: וְכִדְתַנְיָא: הֲרֵי שֶׁהָיָה נוֹשֶׁה בַּחֲבֵירוֹ מָנֶה,
phrases.english: And as it is taught: If someone was owed a מנה by his friend,
phrases.notes: A מנה is one hundred דינרים.

phrases.english: and he went and stood at the friend's granary,
and said: Give me my money,
because I want to buy wheat with it.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ: חִטִּים יֵשׁ לִי שֶׁאֲנִי נוֹתֵן לְךָ,
phrases.english: He said to him: I have wheat that I will give you;

phrases.aramaic: צֵא וַעֲשֵׂה עָלַי כְּשַׁעַר שֶׁל עַכְשָׁיו,
phrases.english: go and calculate what I owe you at today's price,

phrases.aramaic: וַאֲנִי אַעֲלֶה לְךָ כׇּל שְׁנֵים עָשָׂר חֹדֶשׁ –
phrases.english: and I will deliver it to you over the full twelve months.

phrases.aramaic: אָסוּר, דְּלָאו כְּאִיסָּרוֹ הַבָּא לְיָדוֹ דָּמֵי.
phrases.english: It is forbidden, because it is not like a case where his coin came into his hand.
phrases.notes: An איסר is a small coin. The point is that the creditor never handed over even a small coin for this wheat; he only used his old debt.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִדְתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רבה's answer in step 9 with a ברייתא
steps.raayaObject: רבה's claim that turning a debt into a purchase is forbidden
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא forbidding a creditor from taking future wheat at today's price in place of his loan

steps.title: אביי: then even a seller who has wine should be forbidden
steps.stepSummary: אביי objects: if the problem is that no fresh coin was paid, the deal would be forbidden even if the seller has wine, so why does the משנה say he has none?
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: If the reason is that it is not like his coin came into his hand, why does the משנה mention specifically that "he does not have" wine? Even if he does have it, it should also be forbidden!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי challenges רבה's explanation. He says it does not explain the very detail we started asking about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה's reason is that no real money was paid. That problem exists whether or not the seller owns wine. So רבה's answer still leaves the משנה's words "he has no wine" unexplained.

phrases.english: אביי said to him:
If the reason is that it is not like his coin came into his hand,
why mention specifically "he does not have"?
Even if he has it, it should also be forbidden!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי: אִי דְּלָא כְּאִיסָּרוֹ הַבָּא לְיָדוֹ, מַאי אִירְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבה's answer from steps 9 and 10
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's explanation that the problem is the lack of fresh payment
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: That reason applies even when the seller has wine, so it fails to explain why the משנה specifies that he has none.

steps.title: אביי's new approach: read the משנה like רב ספרא's teaching
steps.stepSummary: אביי sets aside רבה's answer and says the משנה should be understood like the teaching רב ספרא brought from the school of רבי חייא about רבית.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, אביי said: Our משנה follows what רב ספרא taught about רבית from the school of רבי חייא.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי offers his own explanation instead of רבה's. This line is a setup: it names the source, and the גמרא will show next how it fits the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since רבה's answer did not explain the detail "he has no wine," אביי turns to a ברייתא that רב ספרא taught from the school of רבי חייא. That ברייתא is about deals that are technically permitted but forbidden as a trick around רבית. The next steps quote it and apply it to the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather; drops the earlier answer for a new one
From the school of רבי חייא

phrases.english: Rather, אביי said:
Our משנה is like what רב ספרא taught
about רבית, from the school of רבי חייא.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: מַתְנִיתִין, כִּדְתָנֵי רַב סָפְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces רבה's answer after אביי's objection in step 11
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה is about paying for wine with an old debt, as רבה said
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה should be understood through רב ספרא's teaching about רבית, explained in what follows

steps.title: The ברייתא of רב ספרא about deals that dodge interest
steps.stepSummary: אביי's source: some deals are allowed on paper but forbidden because they are a trick to get around רבית, like a loan given as wheat and bought back for less.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רב ספרא taught from the school of רבי חייא: some things are permitted yet forbidden, because they are tricks around interest. How so? One asks for a loan of a מנה. The other says he has no cash, but he has wheat worth a מנה. He gives the wheat, then buys it back for twenty-four סלע. This is permitted, but it is forbidden to do it because it is a trick around interest.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now quotes the ברייתא that אביי pointed to in the last step. This is the model he will use to explain the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The borrower now owes a full מנה (100), but he only walked away with 96 in cash after the lender bought the wheat back. Technically these are two separate deals, a loan and a purchase, so the Torah does not forbid it. The רבנן forbid it anyway, because in practice it is a loan of 96 paid back with 100.

keyTerms.meaning: A trick or scheme to get around the ban on interest
Permitted by the strict law, yet forbidden by the רבנן

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read 'permitted and forbidden' as a contradiction. It means the deal is permitted by Torah law but forbidden by the רבנן.

phrases.aramaic: דְּתָנֵי רַב סָפְרָא בְּרִבִּית דְּבֵי רַבִּי חִיָּיא:
phrases.english: As Rav Safra taught, in the laws of interest from the school of Rabbi Chiyya:
There are things that are permitted, yet forbidden
because they are tricks around interest.
How so? One said to him: Lend me a maneh!
He said to him: I don't have a maneh,

phrases.aramaic: חִטִּין בְּמָנֶה יֵשׁ לִי שֶׁאֲנִי נוֹתֵן לָךְ.
phrases.english: but I have wheat worth a maneh that I will give you.
He gave him wheat worth a maneh,

phrases.aramaic: וְחָזַר וּלְקָחָן הֵימֶנּוּ בְּעֶשְׂרִים וְאַרְבַּע סֶלַע –
phrases.english: and then bought it back from him for twenty-four sela.
phrases.notes: Twenty-four סלע is 96 דינרים. So the borrower gets 96 in cash but still owes 100.

phrases.english: It is permitted, yet it is forbidden to do this
because it is a trick around interest.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתָנֵי רַב סָפְרָא בְּרִבִּית דְּבֵי רַבִּי חִיָּיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the source that אביי referred to in step 12.
steps.raayaObject: אביי's new reading of the משנה
steps.raayaSupportSource: ברייתא of רב ספרא from the school of רבי חייא

steps.title: אביי applies the ברייתא to the משנה
steps.stepSummary: The משנה is a 30-דינר loan given as wheat and bought back for a דינר זהב (25). If the borrower pays back with wine, it is fine. If he has no wine and will pay cash, it looks like רבית.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here too: he asked for a loan of thirty דינרים. The other said he had no cash but had wheat worth thirty and gave it to him, then bought it back for a דינר זהב. If the borrower has wine to give for the thirty, the lender is taking produce, and that is no problem. If he has no wine, the lender will surely take money, and that looks like interest.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי fits the משנה into the pattern of the ברייתא. The difference between having wine and not having wine now finally makes sense.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The borrower received only 25 in cash but owes 30. If he repays in wine, the lender is getting produce and not more money, so the רבנן allow it. If he has no wine, he will end up paying 30 in coins for 25 in coins, which looks like רבית. This answers the original question from steps 7–8 about why the משנה says 'he has no wine', which רבה's answer could not explain.

keyTerms.meaning: A gold coin worth 25 silver דינרים

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how the same deal can be fine or problematic depending on whether repayment comes as produce or as money.

phrases.english: Here too, it is a case where he said:
Lend me thirty dinars,

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: שְׁלֹשִׁים דִּינָרִים אֵין לִי,
phrases.english: He said to him: I don't have thirty dinars,

phrases.aramaic: חִטִּין בִּשְׁלֹשִׁים דִּינָרִים יֵשׁ לִי שֶׁאֲנִי נוֹתֵן לָךְ.
phrases.english: but I have wheat worth thirty dinars that I will give you.
He gave him wheat worth thirty dinars,
and then bought it back from him for a gold dinar.
phrases.notes: A דינר זהב is worth 25 silver דינרים, so the borrower gets 25 but owes 30.

phrases.english: If the borrower has wine,
which he gives him in place of the thirty dinars,
then it is produce that he takes from him,
and we have no problem with it.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי לָא, כֵּיוָן דְּלֵית לֵיהּ חַמְרָא –
phrases.english: And if not, since he has no wine,

phrases.aramaic: וַדַּאי מִשְׁקַל זוּזֵי מִינֵּיהּ, מִחֲזֵי כְּרִבִּית.
phrases.english: he will surely take money from him, and that looks like interest.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכָא נָמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the ברייתא from step 13 to the משנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the case of the משנה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה is a simple sale with wine owed, and it is unclear why lacking wine matters.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה is a disguised loan. Repaying in wine is fine, but repaying in cash looks like רבית.

steps.title: רבא: the משנה should have said 'the value of my wheat'
steps.stepSummary: If אביי is right, the lender already bought the wheat back from the borrower, so he cannot ask for 'my wheat'. The משנה should have said 'the value of my wheat'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: If so, instead of 'Give me my wheat', it should have said 'the value of my wheat'!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא starts testing אביי's reading against the exact words of the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In אביי's story, the wheat was already bought back by the lender. So the borrower owes the value of the wheat, not the wheat itself. The משנה's wording 'give me my wheat' does not fit.

keyTerms.meaning: If so (if your reading is right)

phrases.english: Rava said to him: If so,

phrases.aramaic: ״תֵּן לִי חִיטַּי״, דְּמֵי חִיטַּי מִבְּעֵי לֵיהּ!
phrases.english: instead of 'Give me my wheat', it should have said 'the value of my wheat'!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא: אִי הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks אביי's reading in step 14.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The wording 'my wheat' does not fit a case where the wheat was already bought back.

steps.title: Read it as 'the value of my wheat'
steps.stepSummary: אביי adjusts the wording of the משנה to say 'the value of my wheat'.
steps.simpleTranslation: Read it as: 'the value of my wheat'.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers by changing the wording of the משנה to fit his reading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of giving up his explanation, אביי reads the משנה slightly differently so that it fits. This is a small change of words, not a new case.

phrases.english: Read it as: 'the value of my wheat'.

steps.triggerLanguage: תְּנִי ״דְּמֵי חִיטַּי״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבא's challenge in step 15.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה should be read as 'the value of my wheat'.

steps.title: רבא: it should have said 'which I sold you'
steps.stepSummary: The משנה says 'I want to sell it', but in אביי's story the wheat was already sold. It should have said 'which I sold you'.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'As I sell it' — it should have said 'which I sold to you'!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא raises a second wording problem with אביי's reading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In אביי's case, the lender already gave the wheat to the borrower at a value of thirty דינרים. So the lender should describe the wheat as wheat he already sold to the borrower, not as something he still plans to sell.

keyTerms.meaning: As I sell it (a future plan)
Which I sold to you (already done)

phrases.english: 'As I sell it'
should have been 'which I sold to you'!

steps.triggerLanguage: ״שֶׁאֲנִי מוֹכְרָן״, ״שֶׁמְּכַרְתִּים לָךְ״ מִבַּעְיָא לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second wording challenge after אביי fixed the first.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Future tense 'I sell' does not fit a sale that already took place.

steps.title: Read it as 'which I sold you'
steps.stepSummary: אביי again adjusts the wording to 'which I sold to you'.
steps.simpleTranslation: Read it as: 'which I sold to you'.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי fixes the second phrase the same way he fixed the first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Again אביי keeps his explanation and adjusts the words of the משנה to match a sale that already happened.

phrases.english: Read it as: 'which I sold to you'.

steps.triggerLanguage: תְּנִי ״שֶׁמְּכַרְתִּים לָךְ״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבא's challenge in step 17.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה should be read as 'which I sold to you'.

steps.title: רבא: the thirty-דינר price was already set at the start
steps.stepSummary: The משנה has him say 'your wheat is set on me at thirty דינרים', but in אביי's story that price was fixed at the very beginning, so why announce it now?
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Your wheat is set upon me at thirty דינרים' — but from the start, too, it was set on him at this amount!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא raises a third wording problem: the line about thirty דינרים seems pointless in אביי's case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה the thirty-דינר figure sounds like a new valuation made now. In אביי's story, the wheat was already given as a thirty-דינר loan from the first moment, so saying it now adds nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: Set as a debt upon me
He fixed them (the price) upon him

phrases.english: 'Your wheat is set upon me at thirty dinars'
but from the start, too, he set it upon him at this amount!

steps.triggerLanguage: ״הֲרֵי חִטֶּיךָ עֲשׂוּיוֹת עָלַי בִּשְׁלֹשִׁים דִּינָרִין״, מֵעִיקָּרָא נָמֵי הָכִי אוֹקְמִינְהוּ עִילָּוֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third wording challenge.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The thirty-דינר statement is repetitive if the loan was valued at thirty from the outset.

steps.title: He means: wine for the value you set at thirty
steps.stepSummary: אביי explains the line as a reference back to the original price: 'pay me wine for the value of your wheat, which you set on me at thirty'.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what he is telling him: for the value of your wheat that you set upon me at thirty דינר.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers that the line is not setting a new price. It is pointing back to the original one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The borrower is saying that the wine owed will match the thirty-דינר value already fixed at the start. So the line fits אביי's case, because it explains how much wine is owed.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what he is saying to him

phrases.english: This is what he is saying to him:

phrases.aramaic: בִּדְמֵי חִטֶּיךָ שֶׁעָשִׂיתָ עָלַי בִּשְׁלֹשִׁים דִּינָר.
phrases.english: for the value of your wheat that you set upon me at thirty dinar.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכִי קָאָמַר לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבא's challenge in step 19.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The line sets a new price.
steps.terutzMaskana: The line refers back to the original thirty-דינר value as the measure for the wine.

steps.title: רבא: the משנה stresses the market price
steps.stepSummary: The משנה speaks of wine owed when he has none, and it says the wheat went at a כור for a דינר זהב, which was the market price. That wording does not fit אביי's loan-and-buy-back case.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'You have wine with me for them, and he has no wine' — but it teaches 'a כור for a דינר זהב, and that is the market price'!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא raises a final wording problem, and this time אביי gives no answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's language describes a plain sale of wheat at the going market price. אביי's story is a loan of thirty bought back for twenty-five, which has nothing to do with a market-price sale. Since this wording cannot be fixed, אביי's reading is left in trouble.

phrases.aramaic: ״הֲרֵי לָךְ אֶצְלִי בָּהֶן יַיִן וְיַיִן אֵין לוֹ״,
phrases.english: 'You have wine with me for them, and he has no wine'

phrases.aramaic: וְהָא ״בְּדִינַר זָהָב הַכּוֹר וְכֵן הַשַּׁעַר״ קָתָנֵי!
phrases.english: but it teaches 'a kor for a gold dinar, and that is the market price'!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא ״בְּדִינַר זָהָב הַכּוֹר וְכֵן הַשַּׁעַר״ קָתָנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A final wording challenge that goes unanswered.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה's market-price language fits a plain sale, not a disguised loan bought back for less.

steps.title: רבא begins his own explanation
steps.stepSummary: Setting aside אביי's reading, רבא opens his own explanation with the remark that when he dies, רבי אושעיא will come out to greet him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: When I die, רבי אושעיא will come out to greet me,
steps.whatsHappening: The word 'rather' signals that אביי's reading is dropped. רבא is setting up his own explanation, which continues in the next part of the daf.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the last wording problem could not be solved, רבא starts over. He opens with a personal remark about רבי אושעיא. The actual content of his explanation comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: Will come out to greet me

steps.whatToRemember: אביי read the משנה as a loan disguised as a wheat sale. He fixed several wording problems, but the market-price language did not fit, so רבא now offers a new reading.

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:

phrases.aramaic: כִּי שָׁכֵיבְנָא רַבִּי אוֹשַׁעְיָא נְפַק לְווֹתִי,
phrases.english: When I die, Rabbi Oshaya will come out to greet me,

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the unanswered challenge in step 21, רבא drops אביי's approach and begins his own.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: אביי's loan-and-buy-back reading explains the משנה.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבא will offer a different reading, which continues in the next part of the daf.
